title: The Conditions of Entangled Work
author: Richard Claydon
summary: Claydon argues that leadership overwhelm is more often a structural problem than a personal one, caused by different kinds of work being fused into the same roles without ranking or protection. He frames the argument through a composite character, Maya, whose first hundred days reveal unranked demands, defensive reporting and a development offer disconnected from how the organisation actually runs. He distinguishes difficult work from entangled work and sorts loads into Run, Serve and Change, each with its own logic. The hidden cost is named the Confusion Tax, which shows up as coordination theatre, decision latency and eventually moral injury. He contends this burden falls hardest on the coordinating middle, who integrate across boundaries without sovereign authority. Finally he criticises mainstream leadership development as too generic and individual, calling for better diagnosis and practical coherence-building within the work itself.
points: Overwhelm often comes from entangled loads, where Run, Serve and Change work are fused into one role without a rule for which governs when they collide, rather than from sheer volume.
The Confusion Tax is the hidden cost of unclear work, paid in duplicate reporting, pre-meetings, coordination theatre and decision latency that substitute activity for clarity.
The coordinating middle carries the heaviest hidden burden because it is accountable for outcomes it cannot fully control, and conscientious people privatise the contradiction.
Leadership development fails these leaders by offering generic, self-focused uplift built for cleaner first-line or apex roles, so what is missing is fit rather than activity.
quotes: Entangled work is different. It becomes overwhelming because the work is hard to read and hard to rank. Several demands arrive at once, each reasonable on its own terms, but confusing when forced together without enough distinction.
Run work is about continuity, reliability, and control. It keeps the existing operation functioning. It values discipline, repeatability, standards, and dependable execution.

That is how entangled roles so easily produce privatised contradictions. What begins as a structural problem is recoded as a personal burden. The more conscientious the person, the more likely they are to treat the collision as their responsibility to absorb.

Confusion Tax is the hidden organisational burden created when the work is not clear enough to travel cleanly. People are left to work out what is really being asked, which audience matters most, what standard applies, and what has to be translated or softened before anything can move.

Coordination Theatre appears when the organisation responds to confusion by multiplying the visible signs of alignment rather than improving the underlying conditions of work. More meetings are held. More stakeholders are consulted.
This is where the unranked priority list becomes so damaging. When everything matters, every decision becomes politically and morally expensive.
Stress says, “This is too much.” Moral injury says, more quietly, “This is not right, and I am being asked to act as if it is.
